short: A derivative measures how quickly a function changes. On a graph, it is the slope of the tangent line at a point.
medium: Imagine a ball moving along a straight road. Its position changes as time passes, and we can draw that motion on a graph.
The horizontal axis represents time. The vertical axis represents the distance the ball has travelled from its starting point.
Choose two points on the curve and connect them with a straight line. The slope of that line gives the average speed over the interval.
Now slide the second point closer to the first. The interval becomes smaller, and the straight line approaches the tangent to the curve.
The slope of this tangent is the instantaneous speed. This is the derivative of position with respect to time.
A steeper tangent means faster motion. A horizontal tangent means the ball is momentarily at rest. A negative slope means it is moving back.
technical: Bayes' theorem updates a belief when new evidence arrives. We start with a prior probability, then account for how likely the evidence is under each hypothesis.
Suppose one percent of a population has a condition. A test detects ninety nine percent of true cases, but also returns a positive result for five percent of people without it.
Among ten thousand people, approximately one hundred have the condition. Ninety nine of them test positive. Of the remaining nine thousand nine hundred, four hundred ninety five also test positive.
That gives five hundred ninety four positive results in total. Only ninety nine are true cases, so the probability after a positive test is about one in six.
The diagram makes the denominator visible. The positive group contains both true positives and false positives, and the large healthy population contributes many false positives.
This example shows why the base rate matters. A test can be highly sensitive while a positive result still leaves substantial uncertainty.
